prompt: You test which paper plane flies farthest. You change the wing shape — but throw harder when you like a design. Fair test?

choices.text: Fair — wing shape is the only change
Unfair — throw strength also changed
Fair — farther flight proves the design
Unfair — you should change throw strength too

explanation: Two things changed: wing shape and throw strength. You can't tell which made it fly farther.
science_idea: A fair test changes only one independent variable.

prompt: Bigger ice cubes melt slower? Big cube in warm water, small cube in cold water. Spot what's unfair.

choices.text: Changed two things — size and water temperature
Ice always melts the same speed
Only the big cube was unfair
Nothing wrong — clear difference

explanation: Size and temperature both changed, so either (or both) could explain the result.
science_idea: Control variables must stay the same.

prompt: Testing if a heavier marble makes a deeper crater in sand. What is the independent variable (the one you change on purpose)?

choices.text: Depth of the crater
Mass of the marble
Type of sand
How you measure

explanation: Independent = what you change. Dependent = crater depth (what you measure).
science_idea: IV = change; DV = measure; controls = keep the same.

prompt: Same marble crater test. You want a fair test. Which should you keep the same?

choices.text: Only the marble mass
Drop height, sand type, and how you measure
Nothing — change everything for more data
Only the crater depth

explanation: Those are control variables — keep them fixed so only mass explains the crater.
science_idea: Controls isolate the effect of the IV.

prompt: Finish: If I drop a heavier marble from the same height, then the crater will be _____ because _____.

choices.text: deeper, because more mass means more energy on impact
shallower, because heavy things fall slower
the same, because height didn't change
deeper, because sand likes heavy marbles

explanation: Classic If–then–because: one change, a measurable prediction, and a reason.
science_idea: A hypothesis links cause → effect → why.

prompt: More sugar → sweeter tea? You add more sugar and also stir longer each time. What's the problem?

choices.text: Unfair — sugar and stir time both changed
Fair — stirring helps you taste better
Unfair — tea should be cold
Fair — sweetness is easy to judge

explanation: Keep stir time the same so sugar is the only change.
science_idea: Everyday 'tests' often hide extra variables.

prompt: In the tea + sugar test, what is the dependent variable (what you measure)?

choices.text: Amount of sugar
How sweet it tastes
Stir time
Cup size

explanation: DV = sweetness (measured). IV = sugar amount. Controls include stir time, tea type, temperature.
science_idea: Name IV, DV, and controls for every investigation.

prompt: Match each label to the right part of a plant-growth test: 'Does more light make taller seedlings?'

pairs.right: Water, soil, pot size, seed type

choices.text: IV=light, DV=height, Control=water/soil/pot/seed
IV=height, DV=light, Control=water only
IV=water, DV=light, Control=height
IV=soil, DV=pot size, Control=light

explanation: Light is changed; height is measured; everything else stays fixed.
science_idea: Matching IV/DV/controls is the skeleton of any fair test.

prompt: Best hypothesis for: Does a rougher ramp surface slow a toy car?

choices.text: If the ramp is rougher, then the car goes slower because more friction opposes motion
If the car is blue, then it goes faster because blue is speedy
If I like the car, then it will win
If the ramp is higher, then nothing changes because height doesn't matter

explanation: IV (roughness) → predicted DV (slower) → because (friction).
science_idea: Friction converts kinetic energy into heat/sound — stretch link.

prompt:
Imagine two setups drawn side by side:
  Setup A: ball dropped from 1 m into soft sand
  Setup B: same ball dropped from 1 m into hard floor
Question: Is this a fair test of 'does sand softness affect crater depth'? What must stay the same, and what is actually being compared?

choices.text: Fair for surface type — ball, mass, and drop height same; IV = surface softness
Unfair — you must change drop height too
Fair only if the floor also makes a crater
Unfair — same ball means nothing can be compared

explanation: Surface is the IV; height/mass/ball are controls. Hard floor may show 'no crater' — still a valid comparison.
science_idea: Diagrams help spot whether only one thing differs.

prompt: A student says: 'I changed the drop height AND the marble mass to get clearer results.' What should you say?

choices.text: Good idea — more changes = clearer science
Problem — two IVs at once; you can't tell which caused the effect
Fine if you measure twice
Only wrong if the crater gets deeper

explanation: One IV per test. Want both? Run two separate fair tests.
science_idea: Confounding variables muddy the causal story.

prompt: Hypothesis: 'If plants are happier, then they grow taller because happiness helps.' What's weak here?

choices.text: 'Happier' isn't measurable; IV needs a clear, measurable change
Plants don't grow
Height isn't a dependent variable
Nothing — happiness is scientific

explanation: Replace 'happier' with something measurable (hours of light, ml of water, etc.).
science_idea: Operational definitions make variables testable.

prompt: Two balls, same size, different mass, dropped from the same height into sand. Heavier → deeper crater. Best science idea?

choices.text: Heavier balls are 'stronger'
Same height → similar speed; more mass → more kinetic energy on impact
Sand prefers heavy balls
Gravity only pulls light balls

explanation: KE ≈ ½mv². Same speed, larger m → larger KE → deeper crater.
science_idea: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed.

prompt: Same mass, different drop heights. Higher drop → deeper crater. What changed, and why deeper?

choices.text: Height → more speed → more kinetic energy
Height → more mass
Height → less gravity
Nothing about energy; sand just got softer

explanation: Higher drop → more gravitational potential energy → converts to more speed/KE.
science_idea: GPE → KE as the object falls.

prompt: Finish: If I double the drop height (same marble), then the crater will likely be _____ because _____.

choices.text: deeper, because more GPE becomes more KE at impact
shallower, because the marble gets tired
unchanged, because mass stayed the same
deeper, because air always pushes down harder from higher up

explanation: Height stores GPE; impact spends KE. More height → more energy to dig the crater.
science_idea: Energy transfer explains crater depth beyond 'it fell from higher'.

prompt:
Text diagram of energy chain:
  [High shelf] marble → falls → [just before sand] → [crater]
Label the main energy story from shelf to crater.

choices.text: GPE at shelf → KE while falling → work done on sand (crater)
KE at shelf → GPE while falling → light energy in sand
Chemical energy in marble → heat only
No energy change — gravity cancels everything

explanation: Energy isn't destroyed; it transfers: stored (GPE) → motion (KE) → reshaping sand (work/heat).
science_idea: Conservation of energy in a simple chain.

prompt: Student tests 'does wing shape affect glide distance?' Uses three shapes, throws each once outdoors on a windy day, different throwers. Biggest flaw?

choices.text: Many uncontrolled variables: wind, thrower, single trial — hard to trust the pattern
Three shapes are too few ideas
Outdoors is always banned in science
Wing shape can never be an IV

explanation: Repeats, same thrower/strength, calmer conditions (or measure wind) would tighten the fair test.
science_idea: Reliability (repeats) + controls → trustworthy conclusions.

prompt: Match the science word to its job in an investigation.

pairs.right: The one factor you deliberately change
An accidental extra change that muddies results

choices.text: IV=deliberate change; DV=measured outcome; Controls=kept constant; Confound=accidental extra change
IV=measured outcome; DV=deliberate change; Controls=accidental; Confound=kept constant
All four mean 'what you measure'
IV and DV are the same thing

explanation: Stretch vocab: naming a confound shows you can critique a messy test.
science_idea: Precise variable language = clearer thinking.

prompt: Why do scientists often repeat a measurement several times?

choices.text: To spot odd results and see if the pattern is reliable
Because one trial is illegal
To change more variables each time
Repeats replace the need for control variables

explanation: Repeats improve reliability; they don't replace keeping controls constant.
science_idea: Reliability ≠ fair test — you need both.

prompt: Quick check: In 'Does fertilizer amount affect plant height?', fertilizer amount is…

choices.text: Independent variable
Dependent variable
A control variable
Not a variable

explanation: You change fertilizer on purpose → IV. Height → DV.
science_idea: Name the IV from the question wording: 'Does X affect Y?' → X is IV.

prompt: Pick the properly shaped hypothesis:

choices.text: If I water plants more, then they grow taller because water helps cells expand and transport nutrients
Plants are cool so they grow
I think fertilizer is better
Growth happens when stuff

explanation: If (IV) → then (DV prediction) → because (reason).
science_idea: Structure beats vague opinions.

prompt: Claim: 'Heavier always hits harder.' Test: drop a 50 g marble from 50 cm and a 200 g marble from 2 m. What's wrong if we want to isolate mass?

choices.text: Height also changed — mass and energy from height are mixed
200 g is not heavier
Nothing — heavier always wins
Only the light marble is unfair

explanation: To isolate mass, keep height the same. To isolate height, keep mass the same. One IV at a time.
science_idea: Fair tests and energy ideas work together.

prompt:
Text 'lab sketch':
  Cup1: 100 ml water, 1 sugar spoon, stir 10 s, taste
  Cup2: 100 ml water, 3 sugar spoons, stir 10 s, taste
  Cup3: 100 ml water, 5 sugar spoons, stir 30 s, taste
Which cup breaks the fair test, and how?

choices.text: Cup3 — stir time jumped to 30 s while sugar also changed
Cup1 — too little sugar
Cup2 — middle values are always wrong
All fair — water volume matched

explanation: Cups 1–2 keep stir time fixed; Cup3 adds a second IV (stir time).
science_idea: Scan a procedure like a diagram: find the row that breaks the pattern.

prompt: A result disagrees with your hypothesis. Best next move?

choices.text: Check fair test & measurements, then revise or reject the hypothesis — data wins
Delete the data that didn't fit
Change the IV secretly until it matches
Hypotheses can never be wrong

explanation: Science updates ideas when evidence is solid. First verify the method was fair.
science_idea: Hypotheses are tools, not trophies.
